name: Rapeman
label: Touch and Go
lede: Two years, one EP, one album and a band name that drew picket lines in 1988 and that Steve Albini later called indefensible.

eras.title: Big Black ends, Scratch Acid moves north
eras.text: Big Black broke up in 1987 at the top of its game, and Scratch Acid fell apart in Austin the same year. Its bassist and drummer moved to Chicago, and Steve Albini had a new trio within months.

years.h: Steve Albini, David Wm. Sims and Rey Washam form Rapeman
years.p: After Big Black's split, Albini teams with [[David Wm. Sims|c6c8a98f-9cfb-4fad-a657-880245ff15d3]] on bass and [[Rey Washam|33b09380-db28-4c9c-9fdd-ab5c20049c61]] on drums, both just out of Austin's Scratch Acid and newly moved to Chicago.

years.src: Wikipedia: Rapeman · Wikipedia: David Wm. Sims
years.h: Rapeman takes its name from a Japanese manga
years.p: Albini and Washam were fixated on a Japanese comic, The Rapeman, that Albini came across through an import-business contact. According to Wikipedia, the name was meant to repel audiences and thumb its nose at bands chasing MTV.
years.xp:
According to Wikipedia, Albini found the manga repellent and fascinating at once. He later called the name a flippant choice. In a 2020 podcast interview he went further, calling it unconscionable and indefensible, and said he felt he'd never been held to account for it.

Sims, in a 2014 podcast, said he'd always had issues with the name.

eras.title: Picket lines and a cat in the credits
eras.text: Rapeman put out everything that mattered in a single year: an EP half cut live and an album produced, per the sleeve, by Albini's cat. The same months, Albini was becoming the engineer every band wanted, and the name followed the trio to every town.

years.h: Budd EP, Rapeman's first release on Touch and Go
years.p: The seven-minute title track takes its name and language from R. Budd Dwyer, the Pennsylvania state treasurer who shot himself at a televised press conference in 1987. Three of the four songs were recorded live.
years.xp: Pitchfork later ranked Budd sixth on its list of Steve Albini's ten best records, crediting its empty spaces and grainy textures with setting a template for 1990s post-rock.

years.src: Wikipedia: Two Nuns and a Pack Mule
years.h: Two Nuns and a Pack Mule, Rapeman's only album
years.p: Ten songs on Touch and Go (Blast First in the UK), including a cover of [[ZZ Top|a81259a0-a2f5-464b-866e-71220f2739f1]]'s Just Got Paid. Production is credited to Albini and Fluss, later revealed to be Albini's cat.
years.xp: Kerry Crafton engineered. The vinyl sleeve swapped Marmoset and Radar Love Lizard in the track listing, and the CD tacked on the whole Budd EP. FACT later ranked it the 28th best album of the 1980s.
play: Two Nuns and a Pack Mule

years.p: The New Jersey club show on September 24, 1988 survives on tape and is now part of the McKenzie Tapes archive.

years.src: John Peel Wiki · ChicagoPunk Database · Discogs
years.h: John Peel reviews Rapeman at the Mean Fiddler, Harlesden
years.p: Peel wrote up the north London show for The Observer: a miserable choice of name, he said, and a set so intense that plain applause felt faintly insulting.
years.xp:
The name dogged the tour. The Chicago Punk Database says many American shows were met by picket lines of women, and a sold-out show in England nearly got cancelled over a student boycott. By some accounts the controversy only pulled bigger crowds.

A show at Oliver's in Chester on October 12, 1988 was later released as a live record.

eras.title: Split, and three new directions
eras.text: Rapeman ended in 1989 over personal friction, not the name, according to accounts of the band. Its three members went on to shape the next decade of noise rock from Chicago.

years.h: Inki's Butt Crack 7" in the Sub Pop Singles Club
years.p: Rapeman's last release goes out as a Sub Pop Singles Club subscription single.

years.h: Rapeman breaks up; David Wm. Sims starts the Jesus Lizard
years.p: Sims teams back up with his Scratch Acid singer [[David Yow|81af2517-4481-4960-a337-213e1f8b5a61]] in [[The Jesus Lizard|dfebd6c0-dae7-4cc8-a8e9-0dbaa382209f]]. [[Rey Washam|33b09380-db28-4c9c-9fdd-ab5c20049c61]] goes on to the [[Didjits|e3d01dcb-eb41-4ce9-8506-bfd70aa8d651]], [[Ministry|13df2a46-f72f-40e7-aa63-26fcf62c7048]] and [[Helios Creed|26a13357-fad6-4900-a324-ff252e681112]].

eras.title: The engineer and the apology
eras.text: Albini built Shellac and a recording career that ran from the Pixies to Nirvana. Rapeman became the part of his story he stopped defending.

years.h: David Wm. Sims calls Rapeman's name his biggest regret
years.p: In a 2014 podcast, the former Rapeman and Jesus Lizard bassist, by then a New York accountant, says he always had problems with the band's name.

years.h: Steve Albini: naming Rapeman was indefensible
years.p: On a 2020 podcast, Albini calls the name a flippant choice he can't defend, and says he was never held to account for it.

years.h: Steve Albini dies of a heart attack at 61
years.p: Albini died at 61, days before [[Shellac|604f273a-d3c1-4b5b-ab83-99541f9368ea]] released To All Trains. His Electrical Audio studio said the cause was a heart attack.
